katha-1-1-1.translation: Wanting the reward, Vajashravasa gave away all he owned. He had a son named Nachiketas.
katha-1-1-1.meaning: A father makes a big ritual gift, hoping for heavenly reward. His son Nachiketas watches.
katha-1-1-1.explanation: The Katha Upanishad opens with a story. Vajashravasa performs a sacrifice in which he is meant to give away everything, hoping for heaven. His young son Nachiketas is the hero of the tale.

katha-1-1-2.translation: Though only a boy, as the gifts were being led away, faith entered him. He thought:
katha-1-1-2.meaning: As the gifts are taken away, the young boy is filled with faith and begins to think.
katha-1-1-2.explanation: As the cows being given as gifts are led away, sincere faith, shraddha, rises in Nachiketas. He begins to reflect on what he sees.

keywords.meaning: as the gifts were led away

katha-1-1-3.translation: 'These cows have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, given their last milk, and are barren. Joyless are the worlds that one reaches by giving such gifts.'
katha-1-1-3.meaning: Nachiketas sees his father giving away old, useless cows and knows such false giving brings no good.
katha-1-1-3.explanation: Nachiketas notices that his father is giving away worn-out cows that can no longer eat, drink, give milk or bear calves. Giving such gifts while pretending to be generous leads to joyless worlds.

katha-1-1-4.translation: He said to his father, 'Father, to whom will you give me?' He asked a second and a third time. His father said to him, 'To Death I give you!'
katha-1-1-4.meaning: Nachiketas keeps asking his father who he will be given to, and in anger his father says: to Death.
katha-1-1-4.explanation: Hoping to save his father from a false offering, Nachiketas offers himself, asking who he will be given to. He asks three times. Irritated, the father blurts out: 'I give you to Death!'

keywords.meaning: to whom will you give me

katha-1-1-5.translation: Among many I go first; among many I go in the middle. What work does Yama have that he will do through me today?
katha-1-1-5.meaning: Nachiketas wonders what purpose Death could have for him.
katha-1-1-5.explanation: Nachiketas reflects calmly. Among people he is sometimes first, sometimes in the middle. What could Yama, the lord of death, want to do with him today?

katha-1-1-6.translation: Look at how those who came before have gone, and see how those who come after will go. A mortal ripens like grain and, like grain, is born again.
katha-1-1-6.meaning: People are born and die like crops, again and again. Nachiketas accepts this and goes.
katha-1-1-6.explanation: Nachiketas encourages his father to keep his word. All who came before have died and all who follow will too. People ripen and fall like grain, and are born again like grain.

katha-1-1-7.translation: A brahmin guest enters a house like fire. People calm him with an offering. Bring water, son of Vivasvan.
katha-1-1-7.meaning: Nachiketas reaches Yama's house, and a guest must be honoured. Yama's household is urged to bring water.
katha-1-1-7.explanation: Nachiketas goes to Yama's house, but Yama is away for three days. The household is reminded that a holy guest is like fire and must be welcomed. They are told to bring water for him.

katha-1-1-8.translation: Hopes and expectations, good company and kind words, sacrifices and good works, sons and cattle: all these are lost by the foolish man in whose house a brahmin stays without food.
katha-1-1-8.meaning: Neglecting a guest destroys a household's hopes and good fortune.
katha-1-1-8.explanation: This verse stresses the sacred duty of hospitality. If a holy guest stays hungry in someone's home, that person loses hopes, friendships, merit from good deeds, children and wealth.

katha-1-1-9.translation: Yama said: Brahmin, since you, an honoured guest, have stayed three nights in my house without food, I bow to you. May good come to me. In return, choose three wishes.
katha-1-1-9.meaning: Death apologises for leaving his guest without food and offers Nachiketas three wishes.
katha-1-1-9.explanation: Yama returns and finds Nachiketas has waited three nights without food. Honouring him, Yama offers three boons, one for each night.

katha-1-1-10.translation: Nachiketas said: May my father Gautama be calm in mind and cheerful, free of anger toward me, Death. May he greet me with recognition when I am sent back by you. This I choose as the first of three wishes.
katha-1-1-10.meaning: For his first wish, Nachiketas asks that his father be at peace and welcome him home without anger.
katha-1-1-10.explanation: Nachiketas's first wish is not for himself but for his father: that he be calm and kind, no longer angry, and that he recognise and welcome his son when Death sends him back.

katha-1-1-11.translation: Yama said: Auddalaki Aruni will recognise you as before, released by me. He will sleep peacefully at night, free of anger, when he sees you freed from the jaws of death.
katha-1-1-11.meaning: Death grants the first wish: the father will be at peace and welcome his son back.
katha-1-1-11.explanation: Yama grants the first boon. Nachiketas's father, also called Auddalaki Aruni, will recognise him, sleep in peace and feel no anger when he sees his son returned from death.

keywords.meaning: freed from the jaws of death

katha-1-1-12.translation: In the heavenly world there is no fear at all. You are not there, Death, and no one fears old age. Having crossed both hunger and thirst and gone beyond sorrow, one rejoices in heaven.
katha-1-1-12.meaning: Heaven is a place without fear, ageing, hunger or sorrow.
katha-1-1-12.explanation: Nachiketas describes heaven as he understands it: no fear, no death, no ageing, no hunger or thirst, no grief, only joy.

katha-1-1-13.translation: You know, Death, the fire that leads to heaven. Explain it to me, for I have faith. Those in heaven enjoy immortality. This I choose as my second wish.
katha-1-1-13.meaning: For his second wish, Nachiketas asks to learn the sacred fire ritual that leads to heaven.
katha-1-1-13.explanation: Nachiketas's second wish is to learn the fire sacrifice that leads to heaven. He approaches it with faith.

katha-1-1-14.translation: Yama said: I will tell you, Nachiketas. Learn from me this fire that leads to heaven, knowing it well. Know it as the means of attaining endless worlds, as their support, hidden in the secret place.
katha-1-1-14.meaning: Death agrees to teach the fire ritual, which leads to boundless worlds and is hidden deep within.
katha-1-1-14.explanation: Yama agrees to teach the heavenly fire. It is the way to infinite worlds and their foundation, yet it is hidden in the cave of the heart.

katha-1-1-15.translation: He told him about that fire, the source of the worlds: which bricks, how many and how they are laid. Nachiketas repeated it all back as told. Then Death, pleased, spoke again.
katha-1-1-15.meaning: Death teaches the fire ritual in detail, and Nachiketas repeats it perfectly.
katha-1-1-15.explanation: Yama explains the fire altar: the bricks, their number and arrangement. Nachiketas repeats everything accurately, and Yama is delighted.

katha-1-1-16.translation: The great soul, pleased, said to him: I give you another gift here today. This fire will be known by your name. And take this many-coloured chain.
katha-1-1-16.meaning: Pleased, Death names the fire after Nachiketas and gives him a precious chain.
katha-1-1-16.explanation: Delighted with the boy, Yama gives an extra gift: the fire will be called the Nachiketa fire, and he presents a many-coloured garland or chain.

katha-1-1-17.translation: One who has lit the Nachiketa fire three times, joined with the three, and done the three duties, crosses over birth and death. Knowing the adorable God born of Brahman and realising him, one reaches lasting peace.
katha-1-1-17.meaning: Whoever performs this fire ritual with understanding goes beyond birth and death and finds peace.
katha-1-1-17.explanation: Yama praises the Nachiketa fire. One who performs it three times, connected with three teachers or Vedas, and carries out the three duties of sacrifice, study and charity, crosses birth and death and attains supreme peace.

keywords.meaning: having lit the Nachiketa fire three times

katha-1-1-18.translation: One who has performed the Nachiketa fire three times, knowing these three, and who builds the Nachiketa altar with this knowledge, throws off the bonds of death, goes beyond sorrow and rejoices in heaven.
katha-1-1-18.meaning: Performing the fire ritual with understanding frees one from death's ties and sorrow.
katha-1-1-18.explanation: Repeating the praise: one who knows and builds the Nachiketa fire casts off death's snares, passes beyond grief and rejoices in heaven.

katha-1-1-19.translation: This, Nachiketas, is your fire that leads to heaven, which you chose as your second wish. People will call this fire yours. Now choose your third wish, Nachiketas.
katha-1-1-19.meaning: The second wish is granted, and Death asks for the third.
katha-1-1-19.explanation: Yama confirms the second boon. The fire will forever carry Nachiketas's name. He invites the boy to choose his third wish.

katha-1-1-20.translation: There is this doubt about a person who has died. Some say, 'He exists.' Others say, 'He does not exist.' I want to know this, taught by you. This is the third of my wishes.
katha-1-1-20.meaning: For the third wish, Nachiketas asks the deepest question: what happens to us after death?
katha-1-1-20.explanation: Nachiketas's third wish is the central question of the Upanishad. When a person dies, do they still exist or not? He wants the answer from Death himself.

keywords.meaning: about a person who has died

katha-1-1-21.translation: Yama said: Even the gods of old had doubts about this. It is not easy to understand; this matter is subtle. Choose another wish, Nachiketas. Do not press me. Release me from this.
katha-1-1-21.meaning: Death tries to avoid the question, saying it is too subtle even for the gods.
katha-1-1-21.explanation: Yama tests the boy. Even the gods were uncertain about this, he says. It is hard to understand. He asks Nachiketas to choose something else.

katha-1-1-22.translation: Nachiketas said: Even the gods doubted this, and you say it is not easy to understand. But no other teacher like you can be found, and no other wish equals this.
katha-1-1-22.meaning: Nachiketas will not give up: if it is so hard, only Death can teach it, and nothing is more important.
katha-1-1-22.explanation: Nachiketas holds firm. If even the gods doubted and it is hard to know, then he needs a teacher like Yama all the more. No other wish could compare.

katha-1-1-23.translation: Yama said: Choose sons and grandsons who will live a hundred years, many cattle, elephants, gold and horses. Choose a vast stretch of land, and live yourself as many autumns as you wish.
katha-1-1-23.meaning: Death tempts Nachiketas with long life, family, wealth and land instead.
katha-1-1-23.explanation: Yama offers great temptations: long-lived children, cattle, elephants, gold, horses, a large kingdom and as long a life as he wants.

katha-1-1-24.translation: If you think any wish equals this, choose it: wealth and long life. Be great on the wide earth, Nachiketas. I will make you enjoy all your desires.
katha-1-1-24.meaning: Death offers to make Nachiketas rich, long-lived and powerful.
katha-1-1-24.explanation: Yama continues tempting: wealth, long life, rulership over the earth and the fulfilment of every desire.

katha-1-1-25.translation: Whatever desires are hard to get in the world of mortals, ask for all of them as you please. Here are lovely women with chariots and music, such as men cannot obtain. Be served by them, given by me. But, Nachiketas, do not ask about death.
katha-1-1-25.meaning: Death offers every pleasure, if only Nachiketas will stop asking about death.
katha-1-1-25.explanation: Yama's final temptation is every rare pleasure: beautiful companions, chariots and music beyond human reach. Only, he says, do not ask about death.

katha-1-1-26.translation: Nachiketas said: These things last only until tomorrow, Death, and they wear out the vigour of all the senses. Even a whole life is short. Keep your horses, your dancing and singing.
katha-1-1-26.meaning: Nachiketas refuses: pleasures are fleeting, they wear out the senses, and life is short.
katha-1-1-26.explanation: Nachiketas rejects every offer. These pleasures are temporary, they exhaust the senses, and even the longest life is brief. Yama can keep his chariots and entertainments.

katha-1-1-27.translation: A person cannot be satisfied by wealth. We will have wealth if we have seen you. We will live as long as you rule. But the wish I choose is that one alone.
katha-1-1-27.meaning: Wealth never satisfies. Nachiketas wants only the answer to his question.
katha-1-1-27.explanation: Nachiketas explains: wealth cannot satisfy anyone. Having met Death, he will have enough, and he will live as long as Death allows. He still wants only his third wish.

katha-1-1-28.translation: Having come near the undecaying immortals, what decaying mortal on earth, who understands, would delight in a very long life, thinking about beauty, pleasure and enjoyment?
katha-1-1-28.meaning: Once you have glimpsed the eternal, a long life of pleasure loses its charm.
katha-1-1-28.explanation: Nachiketas asks: what mortal, having met the immortals and understanding the truth, would still want a long life of sensual delights?

katha-1-1-29.translation: Tell us, Death, about that which people doubt, what happens in the great passing beyond. This wish, which enters into the hidden mystery, is the only one Nachiketas chooses.
katha-1-1-29.meaning: Nachiketas insists: he wants only to know the hidden truth about what lies beyond death.
katha-1-1-29.explanation: Nachiketas repeats his request with complete determination. He wants to know the great mystery beyond death and will accept nothing else.

katha-1-2-1.translation: Yama said: The good is one thing and the pleasant is another. Both bind a person, with different aims. It goes well for one who takes the good, but one who chooses the pleasant misses the goal.
katha-1-2-1.meaning: Life offers two paths: what is truly good and what is merely pleasant. Choose the good.
katha-1-2-1.explanation: Satisfied by the boy's resolve, Yama begins to teach. There are two paths, shreyas, the good, and preyas, the pleasant. Whoever chooses the good flourishes; whoever chooses the pleasant falls short.

katha-1-2-2.translation: The good and the pleasant both come to a person. The wise examine them and tell them apart. The wise choose the good over the pleasant; the foolish choose the pleasant for the sake of gain and comfort.
katha-1-2-2.meaning: The wise think carefully and pick what is good; the foolish grab what is pleasant.
katha-1-2-2.explanation: Both paths present themselves to everyone. The wise weigh them and choose the good. The foolish choose the pleasant for material gain and security.

katha-1-2-3.translation: You, Nachiketas, after thinking about dear and lovely pleasures, have let them go. You did not take that chain of wealth in which so many people drown.
katha-1-2-3.meaning: Death praises Nachiketas for rejecting pleasures and wealth, which trap so many people.
katha-1-2-3.explanation: Yama praises Nachiketas for having examined and refused attractive pleasures. He has not taken the 'chain of wealth' that traps most people.

katha-1-2-4.translation: Far apart and leading in different directions are ignorance and what is known as knowledge. I see that Nachiketas longs for knowledge; many desires did not tempt you.
katha-1-2-4.meaning: Ignorance and wisdom lead in opposite directions. Nachiketas has chosen wisdom.
katha-1-2-4.explanation: Knowledge and ignorance are far apart and pull opposite ways. Yama sees that Nachiketas desires knowledge, because the many pleasures did not lure him.

katha-1-2-5.translation: Living in the midst of ignorance, thinking themselves wise and learned, fools go round and round, like the blind led by the blind.
katha-1-2-5.meaning: People who think they are wise while lost in ignorance wander like the blind leading the blind.
katha-1-2-5.explanation: Many people living in ignorance believe themselves wise. They wander aimlessly, like blind people led by someone who is also blind.

katha-1-2-6.translation: The passage beyond does not shine for the childish, careless one deluded by wealth. Thinking 'This world is all, there is no other,' he falls again and again into my power.
katha-1-2-6.meaning: Those blinded by wealth, who think this life is all there is, keep dying again and again.
katha-1-2-6.explanation: The way beyond death is not seen by the immature, distracted by money. Believing only in this world, they repeatedly fall into the power of Death.

keywords.meaning: this world, there is no other

katha-1-2-7.translation: Many do not even get to hear of it. Many who hear of it do not understand it. Wonderful is the one who teaches it, and skilful the one who gains it. Wonderful is the one who knows it, taught by the skilful.
katha-1-2-7.meaning: Few hear of the Self, fewer understand it. A real teacher and a real student are both rare.
katha-1-2-7.explanation: The knowledge of the Self is rare. Many never hear of it; many who hear do not understand. A true teacher is a wonder, and so is the student who receives it well.

katha-1-2-8.translation: Taught by an inferior person, it is not easily understood, even if thought about in many ways. Unless taught by another who knows, there is no way to it. It is subtler than the subtle and beyond reasoning.
katha-1-2-8.meaning: This truth cannot be learned from someone who has not realised it, nor by reasoning alone.
katha-1-2-8.explanation: Taught by someone without realisation, this knowledge stays unclear. It needs a teacher who knows. It is subtler than the subtlest and cannot be reached by logic alone.

katha-1-2-9.translation: This understanding cannot be gained by reasoning. Taught by another, it is easily understood, dear one. You have gained it, for you are truly steadfast. May we always find a questioner like you, Nachiketas.
katha-1-2-9.meaning: Truth is not reached by argument but by a teacher. Death wishes all students were like Nachiketas.
katha-1-2-9.explanation: Wisdom does not come from argument. Taught by a realised teacher, it is grasped easily. Yama praises the steadfast Nachiketas and wishes for more seekers like him.

katha-1-2-10.translation: I know that treasure is impermanent, for the permanent is not gained by the impermanent. Yet I built the Nachiketa fire with impermanent things, and so gained what is relatively permanent.
katha-1-2-10.meaning: Temporary things cannot buy the eternal, though they can lead to lasting rewards.
katha-1-2-10.explanation: Yama reflects: worldly treasures are temporary, and the eternal cannot be gained with them. Even he built the fire ritual with impermanent things and reached only his long-lasting position.

katha-1-2-11.translation: Seeing the fulfilment of desire, the foundation of the world, the endless fruit of sacrifice, the shore of fearlessness, great praise and a wide path, you, wise Nachiketas, let them all go with firmness.
katha-1-2-11.meaning: Nachiketas saw every great reward and steadily let them all go.
katha-1-2-11.explanation: Yama lists what Nachiketas has given up: every desire fulfilled, worldly power, endless rewards from ritual, safety, fame and success. He let them go with firm wisdom.

katha-1-2-12.translation: The wise one, knowing through the yoga of inner reflection the ancient God who is hard to see, hidden, deep within, seated in the cave of the heart, leaves behind both joy and sorrow.
katha-1-2-12.meaning: By turning inward, the wise find God in the heart and go beyond joy and sorrow.
katha-1-2-12.explanation: Yama speaks of the Self: hard to see, hidden, dwelling in the heart's cave, ancient. Realising it through inner yoga, the wise go beyond both happiness and grief.

katha-1-2-13.translation: Hearing this and fully grasping it, a mortal who separates the subtle Self from all that is merely right conduct, and reaches it, rejoices, having found what is truly worth rejoicing in. I think the door is open for Nachiketas.
katha-1-2-13.meaning: Whoever truly grasps the subtle Self finds real joy. Death sees that Nachiketas is ready.
katha-1-2-13.explanation: Anyone who hears this teaching, grasps it fully and separates the subtle Self from the body and mind attains true joy. Yama declares that the gate is open for Nachiketas.

katha-1-2-14.translation: Nachiketas said: Tell me what you see beyond right and wrong, beyond what is done and not done, beyond past and future.
katha-1-2-14.meaning: Nachiketas asks Death to describe the reality beyond right and wrong, beyond time.
katha-1-2-14.explanation: Nachiketas asks Yama to describe that which is beyond moral duty and its opposite, beyond cause and effect, beyond past and future.

katha-1-2-15.translation: Yama said: The word that all the Vedas proclaim, that all austerities speak of, and for which people live a disciplined life, I will tell you briefly: it is Om.
katha-1-2-15.meaning: The goal that all scriptures and spiritual practices point to is summed up in one sound: Om.
katha-1-2-15.explanation: Yama answers with the sacred syllable. The goal declared by every Veda, sought through austerity and celibate discipline, is expressed in one word: Om.

katha-1-2-16.translation: This syllable is indeed Brahman. This syllable is indeed the highest. Whoever knows this syllable gains whatever he desires.
katha-1-2-16.meaning: Om is God himself, and knowing it fulfils every true wish.
katha-1-2-16.explanation: Om is not just a sound; it is the imperishable Brahman and the supreme. Knowing it truly brings whatever one seeks.

katha-1-2-17.translation: This is the best support. This is the highest support. Knowing this support, one is honoured in the world of Brahman.
katha-1-2-17.meaning: Om is the best thing to lean on in meditation, and leads to the world of God.
katha-1-2-17.explanation: Om is the finest and highest foundation for meditation. One who knows it is honoured in Brahman's world.

katha-1-2-18.translation: The knowing Self is not born and does not die. It has not come from anywhere and has not become anything. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.
katha-1-2-18.meaning: Your true Self is never born and never dies. It is not destroyed when the body dies.
katha-1-2-18.explanation: This famous verse, also found in the Bhagavad Gita, answers Nachiketas's question. The Self is never born, never dies, came from nothing and becomes nothing. It survives the death of the body.

katha-1-2-19.translation: If the killer thinks he kills, and the killed thinks he is killed, neither of them understands. The Self neither kills nor is killed.
katha-1-2-19.meaning: The true Self is beyond killing and being killed.
katha-1-2-19.explanation: Another verse echoed in the Gita. Anyone who thinks the Self kills or can be killed misunderstands. The Self does neither.

katha-1-2-20.translation: Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the heart of every creature. One free from desire sees it, free of sorrow, through the grace of the Creator, seeing the Self's greatness.
katha-1-2-20.meaning: The Self is tiny and immense, hidden in every heart. Those without craving see it and lose all sorrow.
katha-1-2-20.explanation: The Self is smaller than an atom and larger than the universe, hidden in the heart of each being. A person without selfish desire, by grace and a calm mind, sees its glory and is free from sorrow.

katha-1-2-21.translation: Sitting, it travels far. Lying down, it goes everywhere. Who but me can know that God who rejoices and does not rejoice?
katha-1-2-21.meaning: The Self is still yet everywhere. Only one who knows it within can understand it.
katha-1-2-21.explanation: More paradoxes. The Self is at rest yet reaches far, lying still yet going everywhere. It both rejoices and is beyond rejoicing. Only one who knows can understand it.

katha-1-2-22.translation: Knowing the Self as bodiless within bodies, stable among the unstable, great and all-pervading, the wise do not grieve.
katha-1-2-22.meaning: Seeing the Self as unchanging and everywhere, the wise feel no grief.
katha-1-2-22.explanation: The Self is without a body though it lives in bodies, steady amid all that changes, vast and pervasive. Knowing this, the wise do not grieve.

katha-1-2-23.translation: This Self cannot be gained by teaching, nor by intellect, nor by much learning. It is gained by the one it chooses. To that one the Self reveals its own nature.
katha-1-2-23.meaning: The Self is not found by lectures or cleverness. It reveals itself to those it chooses.
katha-1-2-23.explanation: A key teaching. The Self is not reached through talks, intelligence or study. It reveals itself to those it chooses, to the one who longs for it alone.

katha-1-2-24.translation: One who has not turned from wrongdoing, who is not calm, not focused, or whose mind is not at peace, cannot reach it through knowledge.
katha-1-2-24.meaning: Without giving up wrongdoing and calming the mind, knowledge alone cannot reach the Self.
katha-1-2-24.explanation: Knowledge alone is not enough. One must first stop doing wrong and become calm, focused and peaceful in mind.

katha-1-2-25.translation: For whom priests and warriors are both just food, and death is the sauce, who can know where he is?
katha-1-2-25.meaning: The Supreme takes in everything, even death itself. Who can easily know it?
katha-1-2-25.explanation: A vivid image. For the Supreme, the priests and warriors, the highest classes, are like rice, and death is merely the seasoning. Everything is absorbed into it. How can anyone easily know such a being?

katha-1-3-1.translation: The two who drink the fruit of their deeds in the world of good works, having entered the secret place, the highest dwelling: knowers of Brahman call them shadow and light, as do those who keep the five fires and the three Nachiketa fires.
katha-1-3-1.meaning: Within the heart live two selves: the individual and the Supreme, like shadow and light.
katha-1-3-1.explanation: The third section begins. Two dwell in the cave of the heart: the individual self that experiences the results of action, and the Supreme Self. The wise compare them to shadow and sunlight.

keywords.meaning: the two who drink the fruit

katha-1-3-2.translation: May we master the Nachiketa fire, the bridge for those who sacrifice, and that imperishable, supreme Brahman, the far shore for those who wish to cross to fearlessness.
katha-1-3-2.meaning: The fire ritual is a bridge for worshippers; Brahman is the far shore of fearlessness.
katha-1-3-2.explanation: A prayer to know two things: the Nachiketa fire, a bridge for ritualists, and the imperishable Brahman, the safe shore for those seeking freedom from fear.

katha-1-3-3.translation: Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot. Know the intellect as the charioteer and the mind as the reins.
katha-1-3-3.meaning: Your body is a chariot, your Self the passenger, your intellect the driver and your mind the reins.
katha-1-3-3.explanation: This is the famous chariot image. The true Self is the master riding in the chariot of the body. The intellect is the driver who steers, and the mind is the reins that connect the driver to the horses.

katha-1-3-4.translation: The senses, they say, are the horses, and the objects of the senses are the roads they travel. The wise call the Self, joined with body, senses and mind, the enjoyer.
katha-1-3-4.meaning: The senses are horses running toward pleasures. The Self, joined to body and mind, is the one who experiences.
katha-1-3-4.explanation: Continuing the image: the senses are horses, and sense objects are the paths they run on. The Self, joined with the body, senses and mind, is the experiencer.

katha-1-3-5.translation: One who lacks understanding, whose mind is never held in check, has senses out of control, like the wild horses of a charioteer.
katha-1-3-5.meaning: If your mind is not steady, your senses run wild like untamed horses.
katha-1-3-5.explanation: Without discernment and with an undisciplined mind, the senses run out of control, like bad horses that a driver cannot manage.

katha-1-3-6.translation: But one who has understanding, whose mind is always held in check, has senses under control, like the good horses of a charioteer.
katha-1-3-6.meaning: With a steady mind, your senses obey you like well-trained horses.
katha-1-3-6.explanation: With discernment and a disciplined mind, the senses become obedient, like good horses guided easily by their driver.

katha-1-3-7.translation: One who lacks understanding, whose mind is careless and always impure, does not reach that goal, but returns to the cycle of rebirth.
katha-1-3-7.meaning: Without wisdom and a pure, steady mind, you keep going round in the cycle of birth and death.
katha-1-3-7.explanation: Continuing the chariot image: a traveller whose driver lacks judgement and whose reins are slack never reaches the destination, and is carried back into samsara, the round of rebirth.

katha-1-3-8.translation: But one who has understanding, whose mind is attentive and always pure, reaches that goal from which one is not born again.
katha-1-3-8.meaning: With wisdom and a pure, attentive mind, you reach the goal and are not reborn.
katha-1-3-8.explanation: A traveller with a wise driver and a steady mind reaches the goal, the state from which there is no return to rebirth.

katha-1-3-9.translation: The person whose charioteer is understanding and who holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the road, the highest place of Vishnu.
katha-1-3-9.meaning: A wise intellect guiding a steady mind brings you to the highest goal.
katha-1-3-9.explanation: With discernment as the driver and the mind firmly in hand, the traveller reaches the end of the journey, which the Upanishad calls the supreme abode of Vishnu, the all-pervading.

keywords.meaning: holding the reins of the mind

katha-1-3-10.translation: Higher than the senses are their objects. Higher than the objects is the mind. Higher than the mind is the intellect. Higher than the intellect is the great self.
katha-1-3-10.meaning: There is a ladder inward: senses, objects, mind, intellect, and beyond them the great self.
katha-1-3-10.explanation: The Katha describes levels of reality, rising inward. Sense objects are more fundamental than the senses, the mind than its objects, the intellect than the mind, and the great self (mahat) than the intellect.

katha-1-3-11.translation: Higher than the great is the unmanifest. Higher than the unmanifest is the Person. There is nothing higher than the Person. That is the end, that is the final goal.
katha-1-3-11.meaning: Beyond everything is the Supreme Person. Nothing is higher; that is the final goal.
katha-1-3-11.explanation: The ladder continues: beyond the great self is the unmanifest (avyakta), primal nature; beyond that is Purusha, the Person. Nothing is beyond Purusha. It is the limit and the highest destination.

katha-1-3-12.translation: This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth. But it is seen by those of subtle sight, through a sharp and subtle intellect.
katha-1-3-12.meaning: The Self is hidden in every being, but a sharp, refined mind can see it.
katha-1-3-12.explanation: The Self is concealed in every creature and does not appear openly. Seers with subtle vision perceive it with a focused, refined intellect.

katha-1-3-13.translation: The wise should merge speech into mind, and mind into the knowing self. The knowing self should be merged into the great self, and that into the peaceful Self.
katha-1-3-13.meaning: In meditation, quiet speech into mind, mind into intellect, and intellect into the deep, peaceful Self.
katha-1-3-13.explanation: This verse describes a method of meditation: step by step, draw speech into the mind, the mind into the intellect, the intellect into the great self, and finally rest in the Self of peace.

katha-1-3-14.translation: Arise! Awake! Having found the great teachers, learn. The path is as hard to walk as the sharp edge of a razor, say the wise.
katha-1-3-14.meaning: Wake up and seek wise teachers. The spiritual path is as narrow as a razor's edge.
katha-1-3-14.explanation: One of the most famous calls in the Upanishads, later used by Swami Vivekananda. Rise, wake up, go to the best teachers and understand. The path is difficult, like walking a razor's edge.

katha-1-3-15.translation: Without sound, touch, form, decay, taste or smell, eternal, without beginning or end, beyond the great, unchanging: knowing that, one is freed from the jaws of death.
katha-1-3-15.meaning: The Self has no sound, form or smell. It has no beginning or end. Knowing it frees you from death.
katha-1-3-15.explanation: The Self has none of the qualities the senses grasp: no sound, touch, shape, taste or smell. It is eternal, beginningless, endless, beyond even the great self. Realising it frees one from death.

keywords.meaning: is freed from the jaws of death

katha-1-3-16.translation: The wise one who tells or hears this ancient story of Nachiketas, told by Death, is honoured in the world of Brahman.
katha-1-3-16.meaning: Hearing or telling this story of Nachiketas is itself a blessing.
katha-1-3-16.explanation: The first chapter ends by praising the story itself. Whoever recounts or listens to this timeless tale is honoured in Brahman's world.

katha-1-3-17.translation: One who, being pure, recites this supreme secret in an assembly of brahmins or at the time of the ancestral rites, gains endless reward. It gains endless reward.
katha-1-3-17.meaning: Reciting this secret teaching with a pure heart brings boundless blessing.
katha-1-3-17.explanation: Reciting this sacred teaching in a gathering of the learned or during rites for the ancestors leads to infinite merit. The repetition marks the end of the first chapter.

katha-2-1-1.translation: The self-existent one pierced the openings of the senses outward, so one looks outward, not at the Self within. A wise person, seeking immortality, turned his gaze inward and saw the Self.
katha-2-1-1.meaning: Our senses face outward, so we miss the Self. The wise turn their attention inward.
katha-2-1-1.explanation: The second chapter begins. The Creator made the senses face outward, so people look at the external world. Only a rare wise one, longing for the deathless, turns the eyes inward and sees the Self.

katha-2-1-2.translation: The childish follow outward desires and walk into the wide-spread net of death. But the wise, knowing what is truly immortal, do not seek the lasting among things that do not last.
katha-2-1-2.meaning: Chasing outer desires leads to death's trap. The wise do not look for permanence in passing things.
katha-2-1-2.explanation: Immature people chase external pleasures and fall into death's net. The wise know the immortal and do not expect anything permanent from the impermanent world.

keywords.meaning: among things that do not last

katha-2-1-3.translation: That by which one knows form, taste, smell, sounds, touches and sexual pleasure: by that alone one knows. What remains here that it does not know? This, truly, is That.
katha-2-1-3.meaning: The Self is the one that knows every experience. It is what you have been looking for.
katha-2-1-3.explanation: The Self is the knower behind every sense experience. Nothing escapes it. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

katha-2-1-4.translation: Knowing as the great, all-pervading Self that by which one sees both dreaming and waking, the wise do not grieve.
katha-2-1-4.meaning: The same Self watches both dreams and waking life. Knowing this, the wise do not grieve.
katha-2-1-4.explanation: The Self is the witness of both the dream state and the waking state. Knowing it as vast and all-pervading, the wise are free of sorrow.

katha-2-1-5.translation: One who knows this Self, the experiencer of the honey of life, as the living self close at hand, the lord of past and future, no longer shrinks away from anything. This, truly, is That.
katha-2-1-5.meaning: Knowing the Self as near, as the one who tastes life, and as lord of all time, removes fear.
katha-2-1-5.explanation: Whoever knows the Self as the one who enjoys the fruits of action, as one's own living self, and as the ruler of past and future, no longer fears or recoils. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

katha-2-1-6.translation: He who was born first from austerity, who was born before the waters, who entered the cave of the heart and dwells there, who was seen through the beings: this, truly, is That.
katha-2-1-6.meaning: The first-born of creation, who lives in every heart, is the same as the Self.
katha-2-1-6.explanation: The Upanishad identifies the Self with the first-born creative being, who arose from austerity before the waters of creation, and who now dwells in the heart of all beings. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

katha-2-1-7.translation: Aditi, who arises with life-breath, made of the gods, who entered the cave of the heart and dwells there, who was born through the beings: this, truly, is That.
katha-2-1-7.meaning: Aditi, the mother of the gods, living in every heart, is also the Self.
katha-2-1-7.explanation: Aditi, the boundless mother of the gods, comes forth with prana, the life-breath, and dwells in the cave of the heart. She too is identified with the Self. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

katha-2-1-8.translation: Agni, the knower of all, hidden in the two fire sticks like a child well guarded by pregnant women, is to be praised day after day by watchful people bringing offerings. This, truly, is That.
katha-2-1-8.meaning: The sacred fire hidden in the wood, like a baby in the womb, is the Self.
katha-2-1-8.explanation: Agni lies hidden in the fire-drilling sticks, protected like an unborn child. Each day devoted people tend and praise it. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

keywords.meaning: like a child in the womb

katha-2-1-9.translation: That from which the sun rises and into which it sets, in which all the gods are fixed, beyond which no one goes: this, truly, is That.
katha-2-1-9.meaning: The source from which the sun rises and into which it sets is the Self.
katha-2-1-9.explanation: The Self is the source and resting place of the sun. All the gods depend on it, and nothing goes beyond it. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

katha-2-1-10.translation: Whatever is here is there; whatever is there is also here. One who sees difference here goes from death to death.
katha-2-1-10.meaning: What is here is the same as what is beyond. Seeing everything as separate keeps you in the cycle of death.
katha-2-1-10.explanation: Reality is one: what is in this world is the same as what is in the beyond. Whoever sees only separation keeps passing from death to death.

katha-2-1-11.translation: This is to be grasped by the mind alone: there is no difference here at all. One who sees difference here goes from death to death.
katha-2-1-11.meaning: Use your mind to see that there is no real separation. Seeing division keeps you dying again and again.
katha-2-1-11.explanation: Through a purified mind one must realise that there is no real multiplicity. Seeing separation leads to repeated death.

keywords.meaning: there is no difference here at all

katha-2-1-12.translation: The Person, the size of a thumb, dwells in the middle of the body. He is the lord of past and future. Knowing him, one no longer shrinks away. This, truly, is That.
katha-2-1-12.meaning: The Self lives in the heart, small as a thumb, yet rules all time. Knowing it removes fear.
katha-2-1-12.explanation: The Self is pictured as a thumb-sized person in the heart, the region it is sensed in during meditation. It is the lord of past and future. Knowing it removes fear. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

keywords.meaning: in the middle of the body

katha-2-1-13.translation: The thumb-sized Person is like a flame without smoke. He is the lord of past and future. He is the same today and tomorrow. This, truly, is That.
katha-2-1-13.meaning: The Self is like a clear, smokeless flame, the same today and forever.
katha-2-1-13.explanation: The thumb-sized Self is like a pure, smokeless flame. It rules over all time and does not change from one day to the next. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

katha-2-1-14.translation: As rain falling on a mountain peak runs down the slopes in all directions, so one who sees things as separate runs after them.
katha-2-1-14.meaning: Seeing everything as separate scatters you, like rain running off a mountain.
katha-2-1-14.explanation: As rainwater on a high peak scatters down every slope, the person who sees only separate things runs after them all and is scattered.

katha-2-1-15.translation: As pure water poured into pure water becomes just that, so does the self of the sage who knows, Gautama.
katha-2-1-15.meaning: When pure water is poured into pure water, they become one. So the knower becomes one with the Self.
katha-2-1-15.explanation: A contrasting image: pure water poured into pure water becomes one with it. The self of the knowing sage merges in the same way with the Supreme. Gautama is Nachiketas's family name.

katha-2-2-1.translation: The city of the unborn one, whose mind is straight, has eleven gates. Meditating on him, one does not grieve, and being freed, is freed indeed. This, truly, is That.
katha-2-2-1.meaning: The body is a city with eleven gates, home of the unborn Self. Meditating on it frees you from sorrow.
katha-2-2-1.explanation: The body is pictured as a city with eleven openings, home of the unborn Self whose knowledge never bends. Meditating on it, one is free from grief and, already free, attains final freedom. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

katha-2-2-2.translation: He is the swan in the bright sky, the god in the middle air, the priest at the altar, the guest in the house. He dwells in people, in the highest, in truth, in the sky. Born from water, from cows, from truth, from mountains, he is the great truth.
katha-2-2-2.meaning: The one Self is present everywhere: in sky and air, at the altar and in the home, in people and in nature.
katha-2-2-2.explanation: This verse, from the Rig Veda, lists the many places the one reality dwells: as the sun in the sky, the wind in the air, the fire on the altar, the guest in a home, and in all beings born of water, earth and mountain.

katha-2-2-3.translation: He leads the in-breath upward and casts the out-breath down. All the gods worship the dwarf who sits in the middle.
katha-2-2-3.meaning: The small Self in the heart moves the breath, and all the senses serve it.
katha-2-2-3.explanation: The Self, pictured as a small figure seated in the heart, moves the breaths up and down. All the 'gods', the senses and life-powers, honour it.

katha-2-2-4.translation: When this embodied one, dwelling in the body, slips away and is freed from the body, what remains here? This, truly, is That.
katha-2-2-4.meaning: When the soul leaves the body, nothing living remains. That soul is the Self.
katha-2-2-4.explanation: When the Self leaves the body at death, nothing of life remains in it. That departing presence is the Self. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

katha-2-2-5.translation: No mortal lives by the in-breath or the out-breath. People live by another, on which these two depend.
katha-2-2-5.meaning: We do not really live by breathing. Breath itself depends on something deeper: the Self.
katha-2-2-5.explanation: Breathing in and out is not what truly keeps us alive. Both breaths rest on something else, the Self.

katha-2-2-6.translation: Now I will tell you, Gautama, about this secret, eternal Brahman, and what happens to the self after death.
katha-2-2-6.meaning: Death promises to reveal the secret of Brahman and what becomes of the soul after death.
katha-2-2-6.explanation: Yama now turns directly to Nachiketas's original question: what happens to the self at death? He will explain the hidden, eternal Brahman.

katha-2-2-7.translation: Some souls enter a womb to take on a body. Others go into plants and trees, according to their actions and their knowledge.
katha-2-2-7.meaning: After death, souls take new births according to what they have done and learned.
katha-2-2-7.explanation: Yama explains rebirth. Some embodied beings enter a womb for a new body; others become plants or still things. Each follows their own karma and understanding.

katha-2-2-8.translation: The Person who stays awake in those who sleep, shaping one desire after another: that is the bright one, that is Brahman, that is called the immortal. All worlds rest in it, and no one goes beyond it. This, truly, is That.
katha-2-2-8.meaning: The Self stays awake even while we sleep and dream. It is Brahman, the immortal.
katha-2-2-8.explanation: While the body sleeps, the Self remains awake, creating dreams. It is pure, it is Brahman, it is immortal. All the worlds rest in it. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

katha-2-2-9.translation: As one fire, entering the world, takes the shape of each thing it burns, so the one Self within all beings takes the shape of each, and yet is also outside.
katha-2-2-9.meaning: Like fire taking the shape of what it burns, the one Self appears in every form, yet goes beyond them.
katha-2-2-9.explanation: Fire is one, but appears in as many shapes as the things it burns. Likewise the one inner Self of all beings takes on each form, while also remaining beyond them.

katha-2-2-10.translation: As one air, entering the world, takes the shape of each thing, so the one Self within all beings takes the shape of each, and yet is also outside.
katha-2-2-10.meaning: Like air filling every space, the one Self fills every being, yet goes beyond them.
katha-2-2-10.explanation: The same teaching with the image of air, which fills every space and takes its shape, yet remains one. So does the inner Self.

katha-2-2-11.translation: As the sun, the eye of the whole world, is not stained by the faults of the eyes or of outer things, so the one Self within all beings is not stained by the sorrow of the world, being beyond it.
katha-2-2-11.meaning: The sun is not dirtied by what it shines on. The Self is not stained by the world's suffering.
katha-2-2-11.explanation: The sun lights everything but is not affected by defects in what it lights or in the eyes that see. The Self within all beings is likewise untouched by the world's pain.

katha-2-2-12.translation: The one controller, the inner Self of all beings, who makes his one form into many: the wise who see him within themselves have lasting happiness, and no one else.
katha-2-2-12.meaning: Those who see the one Self within themselves find lasting happiness.
katha-2-2-12.explanation: The one ruler, the inner Self of all, makes his single form appear as many. Only the wise who perceive him in their own hearts gain eternal happiness.

katha-2-2-13.translation: The eternal among the passing, the consciousness of all that is conscious, the one who grants the desires of many: the wise who see him within themselves have lasting peace, and no one else.
katha-2-2-13.meaning: Those who see the eternal Self within, the source of all awareness, find lasting peace.
katha-2-2-13.explanation: The Self is eternal among the impermanent and the awareness within all aware beings. It fulfils the needs of the many. Seeing it within brings eternal peace.

katha-2-2-14.translation: They think: 'This is That,' the indescribable highest joy. How can I know it? Does it shine by itself, or does it reflect light?
katha-2-2-14.meaning: Nachiketas wonders how to know this indescribable joy, and whether it shines by its own light.
katha-2-2-14.explanation: The seekers sense that the Self is the supreme bliss that cannot be described. The question arises: how can it be known? Does it shine on its own, or by borrowed light?

katha-2-2-15.translation: There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars, nor these lightnings, much less this fire. When it shines, everything shines after it. By its light all this is lit.
katha-2-2-15.meaning: The Self is the light behind all light. The sun and stars shine only by its brightness.
katha-2-2-15.explanation: One of the most beloved Upanishadic verses, often chanted at the lighting of lamps. No sun, moon, star, lightning or fire can light the Self. Rather, everything shines because it shines.

keywords.meaning: the sun does not shine there

keywords.word: tam eva bhāntam anu bhāti sarvam

katha-2-3-1.translation: This is the eternal ashvattha tree with its roots above and branches below. That is the bright one, that is Brahman, that is called the immortal. All worlds rest in it, and no one goes beyond it. This, truly, is That.
katha-2-3-1.meaning: The world is an upside-down tree rooted in Brahman above. Brahman is its pure, immortal root.
katha-2-3-1.explanation: This image is later developed in the Gita's fifteenth chapter. The world is an eternal fig tree whose root is above in Brahman and whose branches spread below. That root is pure and immortal. 'This, truly, is That' is the Katha's refrain, pointing back to the Self Nachiketas asked about.

katha-2-3-2.translation: This whole world, whatever there is, came forth from life and moves within it. It is a great terror, like a raised thunderbolt. Those who know it become immortal.
katha-2-3-2.meaning: Everything comes from the living Supreme and moves within it. Those who know it become immortal.
katha-2-3-2.explanation: All that exists has come from prana, the cosmic life, and trembles within it. It is awe-inspiring, like a raised thunderbolt. Those who know it attain immortality.

katha-2-3-3.translation: From fear of it the fire burns. From fear of it the sun gives heat. From fear of it Indra and Wind, and Death as the fifth, run their course.
katha-2-3-3.meaning: Even fire, sun, wind and death do their work in awe of the Supreme.
katha-2-3-3.explanation: Everything in nature follows its law out of reverence for the Supreme. Fire burns, the sun shines, Indra, the wind and death itself all carry out their roles.

katha-2-3-4.translation: If one is able to know it here before the body falls away, one is freed. If not, one must take a body again in the created worlds.
katha-2-3-4.meaning: Try to know the Supreme in this life. If not, you will be born again.
katha-2-3-4.explanation: There is urgency in this verse. Realising the Self in this life, before the body dies, brings freedom. Failing that, one must return to embodiment in the worlds of creation.

keywords.meaning: if able to know it here

katha-2-3-5.translation: As in a mirror, so it is seen in oneself. As in a dream, so in the world of the ancestors. As in water, so in the world of the gandharvas. As shadow and light, so in the world of Brahman.
katha-2-3-5.meaning: The Self is seen most clearly within. In other worlds it is seen only dimly.
katha-2-3-5.explanation: The Self is seen most clearly in one's own purified mind, like a face in a mirror. In the realm of ancestors it is dreamlike, in the realm of celestial beings it is like a reflection in water, and in Brahma's world as distinct as light and shade.

katha-2-3-6.translation: Knowing that the senses are separate, arising and setting on their own, and that their coming and going is distinct from the Self, the wise do not grieve.
katha-2-3-6.meaning: The senses come and go on their own; the Self is separate. Knowing this, the wise do not grieve.
katha-2-3-6.explanation: The senses arise from their own sources and have their own rising and fading. Understanding they are distinct from the Self, the wise are free from sorrow.

katha-2-3-7.translation: Beyond the senses is the mind. Beyond the mind is its essence, the intellect. Beyond the intellect is the great self. Beyond the great is the unmanifest.
katha-2-3-7.meaning: Look deeper: past the senses is the mind, then the intellect, then the great self, then the unmanifest.
katha-2-3-7.explanation: The Katha repeats the inner ladder: from senses to mind, to sattva or intellect, to the great self, to the unmanifest.

katha-2-3-8.translation: Beyond the unmanifest is the Person, all-pervading and without any mark. Knowing him, a person is freed and reaches immortality.
katha-2-3-8.meaning: Beyond everything is the Supreme Person. Knowing him brings freedom and immortality.
katha-2-3-8.explanation: At the top of the ladder is Purusha, pervading all and without any distinguishing mark. Knowing him liberates and grants immortality.

katha-2-3-9.translation: His form is not within the range of sight; no one sees him with the eye. He is revealed by the heart, by wisdom and by the mind. Those who know this become immortal.
katha-2-3-9.meaning: God cannot be seen with eyes, but is known through the heart, wisdom and a still mind.
katha-2-3-9.explanation: The Supreme has no visible form. It is grasped by the heart, by insight and by a disciplined mind. Knowing it brings immortality.

keywords.meaning: not in the range of sight
no one sees with the eye

katha-2-3-10.translation: When the five senses of knowledge are at rest together with the mind, and the intellect does not stir, that is called the highest state.
katha-2-3-10.meaning: When the senses and mind are still and the intellect stops wavering, you reach the highest state.
katha-2-3-10.explanation: The Katha describes the goal of meditation: the five senses come to rest with the mind, and even the intellect ceases to move. That is the supreme state.

katha-2-3-11.translation: This firm holding of the senses is considered yoga. Then one becomes watchful, for yoga comes and goes.
katha-2-3-11.meaning: Yoga is the steady control of the senses. Stay alert, because this state can come and go.
katha-2-3-11.explanation: This is one of the earliest definitions of yoga in Indian literature: the steady restraint of the senses. The practitioner must remain vigilant, since yoga can arise and be lost.

katha-2-3-12.translation: It cannot be reached by speech, by mind or by the eye. How can it be grasped except by one who says, 'It is'?
katha-2-3-12.meaning: The Self cannot be grasped by words, thought or sight. It is known only by affirming that it exists.
katha-2-3-12.explanation: The Self lies beyond speech, mind and sight. The only way in is through firm conviction that it exists.

katha-2-3-13.translation: It should be grasped first as 'It is', and then in its true nature. For one who has grasped it as 'It is', its true nature becomes clear.
katha-2-3-13.meaning: First accept that the Self exists. Then its true nature will gradually become clear.
katha-2-3-13.explanation: Two steps: first recognise that the Self exists. Then its real nature will reveal itself to one who holds that conviction.

katha-2-3-14.translation: When all the desires that dwell in the heart are let go, then a mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman here and now.
katha-2-3-14.meaning: When all desires leave the heart, a mortal becomes immortal and reaches God in this life.
katha-2-3-14.explanation: Freedom comes when every desire lodged in the heart is released. Then the mortal becomes immortal and realises Brahman even in this life.

katha-2-3-15.translation: When all the knots of the heart are cut here, then a mortal becomes immortal. This is the whole of the teaching.
katha-2-3-15.meaning: When the knots in the heart are untied, you become immortal. That is the whole teaching.
katha-2-3-15.explanation: The 'knots of the heart' are the bonds of ignorance and desire. When they are cut, the mortal becomes immortal. This, Yama says, is the entire teaching.

katha-2-3-16.translation: There are a hundred and one channels of the heart. One of them goes up to the crown of the head. Going up by it, one reaches immortality. The others lead in all directions at the time of death.
katha-2-3-16.meaning: At death, the soul that leaves through the channel to the crown reaches immortality.
katha-2-3-16.explanation: The Katha describes a teaching about death. Of the heart's many channels, one rises to the top of the head. The soul departing through it reaches immortality; the others lead in various directions to rebirth.

katha-2-3-17.translation: The thumb-sized Person, the inner Self, always dwells in the hearts of people. One should draw him out from one's own body with steadiness, like a reed from its sheath. Know him as bright and immortal. Know him as bright and immortal.
katha-2-3-17.meaning: With patience, separate the Self from the body, like pulling a reed from its husk. It is bright and immortal.
katha-2-3-17.explanation: A vivid image of discrimination. The Self in the heart should be separated in understanding from the body, carefully, as one draws the inner stem from a munja grass reed. It is pure and deathless.

keywords.meaning: like a reed from its sheath

katha-2-3-18.translation: Having received this knowledge taught by Death, and the whole practice of yoga, Nachiketas reached Brahman, became free of impurity and free of death. So will anyone else who knows the Self in this way.
katha-2-3-18.meaning: Nachiketas learned from Death, reached God and became free. Anyone who learns this can do the same.
katha-2-3-18.explanation: The Katha ends with the result. Nachiketas, having received the full teaching and method of yoga from Death, attained Brahman and became pure and deathless. The same awaits anyone who knows the Self this way.
